scope: All fifteen open GitHub reports titled [Missing entry] between issues 69 and 86.
editorial_rule: The reports are prompts for research, not evidence. Only claims supported by the cited public records enter the profiles or graph.

profiles.title: Eric L. Trist
profiles.summary: Eric Lansdown Trist was a central figure in the development of sociotechnical systems and organisation design. The cited chapter abstract connects his work with action research and Fred Emery; a public practice source provides a route into his account of the evolution of the sociotechnical systems idea.
profiles.why: Trist's work makes the design of work inseparable from the design of its technologies and social arrangements.
distinctions: Sociotechnical inquiry is not a request to optimise a social subsystem and a technical subsystem separately.
Collaboration with Fred Emery does not make every later sociotechnical claim jointly authored.
lineage: Tavistock action research and the development of sociotechnical systems.
practice: Examine the work system, technical arrangements, discretion, and coordination together.
misreadings: The sources support contribution and collaboration, not the report's stronger language of proof or sole invention.
checks: The full Palgrave chapter was not read in this pass; detailed Penn, York, Ackoff, and Hawk lineage claims need their own primary locators.
profiles.outcome: profile_deepened; bounded contribution retained; unverified academic-lineage claims excluded

profiles.title: James J. Kay
profiles.summary: James J. Kay worked in environment and resource studies at the University of Waterloo. The Ecosystem Approach credits him with chapters on systems thinking, system description, management, and self-organising holarchic open systems.
profiles.why: Kay offers a route into ecological inquiry which joins systems description, uncertainty, self-organisation, and the practical problem of managing for sustainability.
distinctions: A chapter title establishes authorship and topic, not the truth of a thermodynamic law or a complete method.
Ecosystem self-organisation and policy prescription are different kinds of claim.
lineage: Ecological systems, complexity, thermodynamics, and the ecosystem approach.
practice: Treat descriptions of an ecosystem, choices about management, and claims about sustainability as connected but non-identical.
misreadings: The submitted influence list is not reproduced as a verified intellectual genealogy.
checks: Full-text review is still needed for the proposed Prigogine, Odum, Wicken, Koestler, Funtowicz, and Ravetz connections.
profiles.outcome: profile_deepened; publication contribution retained; broad influence claims deferred

profiles.title: David L. Hawk
profiles.summary: David L. Hawk wrote the 2020 proceedings paper Socio-technical-natural systems thinking. Its abstract revisits socio-technical concerns through the environmental context of industrial activity and identifies Trist's work as a point of departure.
profiles.why: Hawk's paper asks what is omitted when a sociotechnical frame treats the natural environment as background rather than as part of the system under consideration.
distinctions: Citing or discussing Trist and Ackoff is not evidence of studying under them.
A publication abstract supports the paper's stated concern, not every biographical claim in the report.
lineage: A proposed extension from sociotechnical to socio-technical-natural inquiry.
practice: Test whether an organisational intervention has pushed ecological effects outside its chosen boundary.
misreadings: The entry does not present Hawk as a simple conduit from a single Penn lineage.
checks: The full paper and primary records for the Penn, Stockholm, and named collaborator claims remain to be reviewed.
profiles.outcome: profile_deepened; paper-level claim retained; teacher-student and collaboration claims deferred

profiles.title: Ian I. Mitroff
profiles.summary: Ian I. Mitroff worked across crisis management, organisational inquiry, wicked problems, and applied epistemology. Berkeley's Center for Catastrophic Risk Management records his senior research affiliation and describes a career concerned with preparing organisations for multiple kinds of crisis; he is also a credited author of Tools, Exercises, and Strategies for Coping With Complexity.
profiles.why: Mitroff's work keeps inquiry into what problem is being addressed close to the organisational capacity to anticipate, contain, recover from, and learn through crises.
distinctions: A named crisis-management framework is not identical to a general theory of systems.
Asking whether the right problem has been formulated is distinct from finding a better solution to the stated problem.
lineage: Systems inquiry, organisational crisis management, and wicked-problem research.
practice: Before solving a declared problem, test the assumptions which made that problem formulation appear natural.
misreadings: The profile does not confer sole authorship of every idea later associated with crisis management or Type III error.
checks: Specific framework stages, Churchman lineage, and claims of priority require publication-level locators.
profiles.outcome: full_profile_added; institutional and publication record retained; priority claims excluded

profiles.title: Gary S. Metcalf
profiles.summary: Gary S. Metcalf is a systems researcher and co-editor of the 2021 Handbook of Systems Sciences. ISSS records his presidency, while IFSR lists him among its fellows; these records establish editorial and institutional roles without substituting them for analysis of his published arguments.
profiles.why: His documented roles give readers an entrance into contemporary attempts to connect systems-science traditions, education, and practice.
distinctions: Editing a handbook is a contribution to a field's conversation, not authorship of every chapter.
Institutional office and intellectual merit require separate evidence.
lineage: Contemporary systems-sciences publishing and professional institutions.
practice: Use the Handbook as a plural collection, retaining differences between its contributors rather than treating it as one doctrine.
misreadings: The entry does not reproduce the report's broad claims about second-wave systems thinking without named publications.
checks: The report's claims about social systems design, Banathy, and specific philosophical contributions remain publication-level research tasks.
profiles.outcome: full_profile_added; editorial and office roles retained; broad intellectual claims deferred

profiles.title: Timothy F. H. Allen
profiles.summary: Timothy F. H. Allen was a biological theorist of complexity whose University of Wisconsin profile identifies hierarchy theory, ecological economics, and sustainability among his concerns. He co-authored Hierarchy Theory with Valerie Ahl, contributed a chapter on scale and type to The Ecosystem Approach, and served as ISSS president in 2008–09.
profiles.why: Allen's work offers a disciplined way to ask how the scale, rate, and observer's chosen level alter what counts as a system and what can be said about it.
distinctions: Hierarchy theory concerns observation and organisation across scales; it need not imply a chain of command.
Allen's contribution must retain Valerie Ahl's co-authorship.
lineage: Hierarchy theory, ecology, complexity, and systems science.
practice: State the scale and rate at which a pattern is being observed before drawing conclusions across levels.
misreadings: The profile does not turn a university expert summary into a complete account of hierarchy theory.
checks: The books' arguments and the submitted claims about influence on other named scholars still require close reading.
profiles.outcome: profile_deepened; hierarchy, ecology, and office records retained; influence claims deferred

profiles.title: Peter H. Jones
profiles.summary: Peter H. Jones works in systemic design, healthcare design, and dialogic inquiry. OCAD University identifies him as a co-founder of the Systemic Design Association and describes work on information services and complex social systems; Tecnológico de Monterrey announced his Faculty of Excellence appointment in March 2024.
profiles.why: Jones's work supplies a concrete bridge between systems inquiry and design practice in services, policy, healthcare, and collective deliberation.
distinctions: Systemic design is not established as one person's invention by a co-founder role.
A dated appointment announcement and an undated institutional biography do not establish permanent current roles.
lineage: Systemic design, dialogic design, service design, and healthcare design.
practice: Bring boundary, stakeholder, service, and information questions into the design process rather than treating design as object production alone.
misreadings: The submitted description's language of a foundational figure and codification is treated as a proposal, not an accepted ranking.
checks: Claims about founding priority, named collaborations, and method development need publication or organisational records.
profiles.outcome: profile_deepened; institutional roles and practice areas retained; priority language qualified

profiles.title: Michael Lissack
profiles.summary: Michael Lissack describes his work as applied philosophy, cybernetics, and second-order science, with attention to the observer, modelling, anticipation, and unexamined presuppositions. The American Society for Cybernetics records his presidency from 2014 to 2020.
profiles.why: His current programme makes the observer's commitments, exclusions, and consequences part of the inquiry rather than invisible background.
distinctions: An author-maintained profile establishes his stated programme, not independent acceptance of its concepts.
Second-order inquiry is not permission to make evidence optional.
lineage: Second-order cybernetics, anticipatory systems, and philosophy of inquiry.
practice: Surface the presuppositions which allow a model or explanation to count as adequate for its observer.
misreadings: The profile does not accept the report's broad claims about complexity theory without source-level argument review.
checks: Individual concepts and current in-press work need their published texts before stronger conceptual edges are added.
profiles.outcome: profile_deepened; self-described programme and office record retained; theoretical validation left open

profiles.title: Kyoichi (Jim) Kijima
profiles.summary: Kyoichi Kijima is a systems scientist working across systems methodology, decision systems, and service systems. He co-edited the 2021 Handbook of Systems Sciences, and ISSS records his presidency; his laboratory biosketch supplies an author-maintained account of his research and institutional work.
profiles.why: Kijima's documented work gives readers a route from systems-science institutions and methods into the study of service and decision systems.
distinctions: Service science is not reducible to customer service or to one systems methodology.
A handbook editorship and presidency are roles, not proof of conceptual priority.
lineage: Systems methodology, decision systems, service systems, and systems-sciences institutions.
practice: Treat service as a system of interacting actors, resources, purposes, and institutional arrangements.
misreadings: The report's claims of foundational status and global expansion are not retained as settled rankings.
checks: Specific methods, collaborations, and claimed service-science innovations need close reading of named publications.
profiles.outcome: full_profile_added; research areas, editorship, and office retained; ranking claims excluded

profiles.title: Gerald Midgley
profiles.summary: Gerald Midgley is a systems researcher associated with systemic intervention, boundary critique, methodological pluralism, and the study of marginalisation. His own account of systemic intervention and institutional profiles establish these areas of work; ANU and ISSS also record his 2013–14 presidency of ISSS.
profiles.why: Midgley's work connects choices about system boundaries and methods with questions of value, marginalisation, and who participates in an intervention.
distinctions: Methodological pluralism requires a rationale for combining methods; it is not a miscellaneous toolkit.
Boundary choices are practical and ethical judgements, not merely diagram edges.
lineage: Critical systems thinking, boundary critique, and systemic intervention.
practice: Ask whose concerns are centred, whose are marginalised, and how method choice changes the intervention.
misreadings: The profile does not attribute every later framework influenced by Midgley to him as its author.
checks: Claims of collaboration or influence outside the cited records remain separate, source-specific questions.
profiles.outcome: full_profile_added; established contribution and office retained; derivative claims bounded

profiles.title: Judith Rosen
profiles.summary: Judith Rosen contributed an introduction and a short story about Robert Rosen to the second edition of Anticipatory Systems (2012). Springer identifies Robert Rosen as the book's author and describes her contributions separately.
profiles.why: Her credited contributions form part of how a later edition presents Robert Rosen's work and its personal and intellectual context.
distinctions: Contributing to an edition is not authorship of the original book or its central theory.
Family relationship, editorial labour, scholarship, and theoretical extension are distinct claims.
lineage: The publication and reception history of Robert Rosen's Anticipatory Systems.
practice: Credit the contribution named by the publisher without inflating or erasing it.
misreadings: The report's wider claims about preservation, translation, ecology, cognition, and health are not established by the publisher record.
checks: Judith Rosen's wider publications and any Rosen Enterprises archive role need separate, public, publication-level evidence.
profiles.outcome: profile_deepened; exact contribution retained; wider scholarly claims deferred

profiles.title: Robert Rosen
profiles.summary: Robert Rosen was a theoretical biologist whose work addressed relational biology, anticipatory systems, modelling, and the organisation of living systems. His scientific-work archive provides routes into the corpus; Springer identifies him as the author of Anticipatory Systems, and ISSS records his presidency in 1980–81.
profiles.why: Rosen matters to systems inquiry because he treated modelling and anticipation as constitutive questions for living organisation, not merely as techniques for forecasting it.
distinctions: Anticipation is not the same as prediction.
A modelling relation is not interchangeable with a computer simulation.
An archive landing page locates a corpus; it does not settle interpretations of Rosen's mathematics.
lineage: Relational biology, mathematical biology, and anticipatory systems.
practice: Distinguish a model used by an anticipatory organisation from an observer's external simulation of that organisation.
misreadings: The entry does not repeat the report's claim that Rosen proved living systems cannot be simulated; that stronger formulation needs exact textual and mathematical treatment.
checks: A close-reading pass is still required for the modelling relation, (M,R)-systems, closure to efficient causation, and claims about complexity.
profiles.outcome: full_profile_added; corpus, authorship, and office retained; strong mathematical claims reserved for close reading

profiles.title: Allenna Leonard
profiles.summary: Allenna Leonard is a practitioner of organisational cybernetics. Her 2014 conference biography describes using the Viable System Model and Team Syntegrity and working with Stafford Beer. ASC records her 2002–04 presidency, and ISSS records her later presidency.
profiles.why: Leonard provides a documented route from management cybernetics into organisational consulting, facilitation, and the stewardship of cybernetics institutions.
distinctions: Using and adapting a method is distinct from originating it.
Institutional leadership and theoretical contribution need separate evidence.
lineage: Management cybernetics, the Viable System Model, Team Syntegrity, and professional societies.
practice: Use VSM and Team Syntegrity as explicit practices whose application and consequences can be examined, not as prestige labels.
misreadings: The entry does not infer every named collaboration or claim of method refinement from a conference biography.
checks: Metaphorum, Systems Thinking Ontario, IFSR Conversation, and later publication claims need their own organisational or publication records.
profiles.outcome: profile_deepened; method use, collaboration, and office roles retained; wider network claims deferred

profiles.title: International Society for the Systems Sciences
profiles.summary: The International Society for the Systems Sciences is an interdisciplinary society whose own history traces its origin to the Society for General Systems Research and mid-1950s meetings associated with the AAAS. It convenes annual meetings, records a long succession of presidents, and is an IFSR member organisation.
profiles.why: ISSS is one of the durable institutional places through which systems-science traditions have met, argued, published, and reproduced themselves.
distinctions: A society can host a field without speaking for all of it.
Institutional continuity does not establish one unified systems doctrine or an unbroken line from the Macy conferences.
lineage: The Society for General Systems Research, annual systems-sciences meetings, and later ISSS institutional history.
practice: Use the society's records to locate people, meetings, and publications, while checking substantive claims in their primary texts.
misreadings: The report's claims that ISSS unified the field, eliminated duplication, or created a shared language are institutional aspirations, not demonstrated outcomes.
checks: The exact constitutional history, AAAS affiliation, founders, name-change dates, and the claimed relationship to the Macy conferences merit a separate archival pass.
profiles.outcome: full_profile_added; institutional history and membership retained; totalising impact claims rejected

profiles.title: International Federation for Systems Research
profiles.summary: The International Federation for Systems Research is a federation of systems and cybernetics organisations founded in 1980. Its official account describes a mission to advance research, support practice, connect member organisations, convene conversations, and promote international cooperation and publication.
profiles.why: IFSR gives the field a network-of-organisations form and a recurring setting for cross-tradition conversation which no single member society could supply alone.
distinctions: A peak-body claim describes an institutional role, not authority over the whole field.
Membership, collaboration, journal relationships, and control of a publication are different relations.
lineage: International federation-building across systems science and cybernetics since 1980.
practice: Use federation records to locate organisations and conversations while preserving differences among members.
misreadings: The report's claims about preventing duplication, academic standards, encyclopaedia maintenance, and a single contemporary agenda exceed the located evidence.
checks: Founding-member records, the full journal relationship, book-series governance, and leadership chronology need document-level verification.
profiles.outcome: full_profile_added; mission, foundation, membership, and conversations retained; unsupported governance claims excluded
